stem: Which one of the following describes a system of agriculture where a single crop is grown on a large area?
solution:
**(b) Plantation Agriculture.**

Plantation is a type of commercial farming in which a **single crop is grown on a large area**. It covers large tracts of land, uses capital-intensive inputs and migrant labourers, and the whole produce is used as raw material in the respective industry. Tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana are important plantation crops in India.
groundedIn: § Commercial Farming — plantation is a type of commercial farming in which a single crop is grown on a large area, covering large tracts of land with capital intensive inputs and migrant labourers.

stem: Which one of the following is a rabi crop?
solution:
**(b) Gram.**

Rabi crops are sown in winter from October to December and harvested in summer from April to June. The important rabi crops are **wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard**.

Rice, millets and cotton are kharif crops, grown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October.
groundedIn: § Cropping Pattern — the important rabi crops are wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard, while paddy, cotton and the millets jowar and bajra are listed among the kharif crops.

stem: Which one of the following is a leguminous crop?
solution:
**(a) Pulses.**

Pulses are leguminous crops. Being leguminous, all of them except arhar help in **restoring soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air**, and so they are mostly grown in rotation with other crops. Major pulses grown in India are tur (arhar), urad, moong, masur, peas and gram.

Jowar and the other millets are coarse grains, and sesamum is an oil seed.
groundedIn: § Major Crops — the pulses paragraph states that, being leguminous crops, all of them except arhar help in restoring soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air, and jowar is listed among the millets; § Food Crops other than Grains — the oil seeds paragraph lists sesamum (til) among the main oil seeds produced in India.

context: Answer the following questions in 30 words.
stem: Name one important beverage crop and specify the geographical conditions required for its growth.
solution:
**Tea** is an important beverage crop.

Geographical conditions required:

1. **Climate** — tropical and sub-tropical, warm and moist and frost-free all through the year.
2. **Rainfall** — frequent showers evenly distributed over the year, for the continuous growth of tender leaves.
3. **Soil** — deep and fertile well-drained soil, rich in humus and organic matter.
4. **Labour** — abundant, cheap and skilled labour, as tea is labour-intensive.
groundedIn: § Food Crops other than Grains — the tea paragraph: tea grows well in tropical and sub-tropical climates with deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus and organic matter, needs a warm, moist, frost-free climate with frequent showers evenly distributed over the year, and is labour-intensive, requiring abundant, cheap and skilled labour.

context: Answer the following questions in 30 words.
stem: Name one staple crop of India and the regions where it is produced.
solution:
**Rice** is the staple food crop of a majority of the people in India.

Regions of production:

1. The **plains of north and north-eastern India**, the **coastal areas** and the **deltaic regions**.
2. **Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan**, where canal irrigation and tubewells have made rice possible in areas of less rainfall.
groundedIn: § Major Crops — rice is the staple food crop of a majority of the people in India, grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, the coastal areas and the deltaic regions, and in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan through canal irrigation and tubewells.

context: Answer the following questions in 30 words.
stem: Enlist the various institutional reform programmes introduced by the government in the interest of farmers.
solution:
Institutional reform programmes introduced in the interest of farmers:

1. **Collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari**, taken up after Independence.
2. **Land reform**, the main focus of the First Five Year Plan.
3. **Crop insurance** against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease.
4. **Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks** giving loans at lower rates of interest.
5. **Kissan Credit Card (KCC)** and the **Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS)**.
6. **Minimum support price, remunerative and procurement prices** for important crops, to check exploitation by speculators and middlemen.
groundedIn: § Technological and Institutional Reforms — collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari; land reform as the focus of the First Five Year Plan; crop insurance, Grameen banks and cooperative societies, Kissan Credit Card and Personal Accident Insurance Scheme, and the announced minimum support, remunerative and procurement prices.

context: Answer the following questions in about 120 words.
stem: Suggest the initiative taken by the government to ensure the increase in agricultural production.
solution:
The government has taken both **institutional** and **technical** initiatives.

1. **Institutional reforms after Independence** — collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari; land reform was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan, and consolidation of holdings was needed because the right of inheritance had fragmented land holdings.
2. **Technical reforms of the 1960s and 1970s** — the **Green Revolution**, based on a package technology, and the **White Revolution (Operation Flood)**.
3. **Comprehensive land development programme of the 1980s and 1990s** — institutional and technical reforms together, because the earlier strategies had concentrated development in a few selected areas. It provided **crop insurance** against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease, and set up **Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks** to give farmers loans at lower rates of interest.
4. **Schemes and information** — the **Kissan Credit Card (KCC)** and the **Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS)**, and special weather bulletins and agricultural programmes for farmers on radio and television.
5. **Price support** — the government announces **minimum support price, remunerative and procurement prices** for important crops to check the exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen.
groundedIn: § Technological and Institutional Reforms — the account of collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari, land reform in the First Five Year Plan, the Green Revolution and White Revolution (Operation Flood) of the 1960s and 1970s, the comprehensive land development programme of the 1980s and 1990s with crop insurance and Grameen banks, and the Kissan Credit Card, Personal Accident Insurance Scheme, weather bulletins and announced support prices.

context: Answer the following questions in about 120 words.
stem: Describe the geographical conditions required for the growth of rice.
solution:
Rice is the **staple food crop** of a majority of the people in India, and India is the second largest producer of rice in the world after China.

Geographical conditions required:

1. **Season** — it is a **kharif crop**, sown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October.
2. **Temperature** — high temperature, **above 25\(^\circ\)C**.
3. **Humidity** — high humidity through the growing period.
4. **Rainfall** — annual rainfall **above 100 cm**. In areas of less rainfall it grows with the help of **irrigation**.
5. **Areas of cultivation** — it is grown in the **plains of north and north-eastern India**, the **coastal areas** and the **deltaic regions**.

The development of a dense network of **canal irrigation and tubewells** has made it possible to grow rice even in the areas of less rainfall such as Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.
groundedIn: § Major Crops — rice is a kharif crop requiring high temperature above 25 degrees Celsius and high humidity with annual rainfall above 100 cm, grows with irrigation where rainfall is less, and is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, the coastal areas and the deltaic regions, with canal irrigation and tubewells extending it to Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.
